items.title: OpenAI's Codex CLI 0.171.0 turns on a TUI workspace by default — previews, subagent transcripts, and remote session control
items.summary: The terminal UI now ships with searchable document previews, image previews, and subagent transcripts alongside the main conversation, on by default. Also new: codex exec --remote <ADDR> to start or resume noninteractive sessions on an existing app server, and /rc / /remote to manage remote control and pair a display device from the TUI.
items.why: This is OpenAI making the terminal workspace itself more like an IDE — you can now actually see what a subagent did without tailing logs, and drive a session from a different machine.
items.action: Update Codex CLI, open a multi-step task and check the new subagent-transcript panel — then try codex exec --remote against a long-running session from a second machine.

eval.reason: Default-on TUI redesign (previews + subagent transcripts) plus new remote session/device-pairing commands; genuine capability change, re-checked not a duplicate of any prior pick in the last 14 days.

items.title: Claude Code ships easel, a built-in mod that draws charts on request and under MCP metrics results

items.title: OpenAI's chief scientist proposes perplexity, not benchmarks, as the shared metric for pacing AI progress
items.summary: Jakub Pachocki publishes OpenAI's internal perplexity measurements going back to GPT-3.5 and argues for perplexity (cross-entropy loss) as a common metric across labs, with progress beyond agreed thresholds gated on the industry's ability to understand model behavior. Sam Altman amplified it as the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while. This is discourse, not a shipped product.
items.why: If labs converge on this, capability claims stop being a benchmark-marketing contest and start being tied to a harder-to-game, continuously tracked number.
items.action: Next time a lab claims a capability jump, ask whether they show the perplexity delta behind it, not just the benchmark score.

eval.reason: Genuine research/governance publication from OpenAI's chief scientist with real data (perplexity vs. capability across model generations), not a duplicate, not pricing/benchmark-only.
Re-fetched openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/ fresh at eval time; dated 2026-11-22, resolves to the post.
Summary reflects the post's own stated thesis and chart, read directly.
Not a SHIPPED item.

items.title: LangChain: what actually breaks when you move agents from prompted to proactive
items.summary: Sydney Runkle describes the architecture behind LangChain's own internal GTM Agent and Robin (their engineering agent, formerly Open SWE) — both built on Managed Deep Agents, where over 70% of runs now start from a schedule or event rather than a human prompt. The real lesson is memory: a three-part model of seed, feedback, and outcomes, and why salience, expiry, and duplication are the hard parts of keeping that memory useful as it grows.
items.why: This is the concrete version of 'give your agent memory' — a specific breakdown of what to store and when it goes stale, from a team running it in production.
items.action: Pick one coding agent you run on a schedule or trigger and write down, in the seed/feedback/outcomes framing, what it's actually remembering between runs today.

eval.reason: Real production data (>70% of Deep Agent runs now schedule/event-triggered) and a concrete memory architecture; checked against the last 14 days, not a duplicate of the already-used knowledge-factory (11-21/22) or LangSmith-ROI (11-20) posts.

items.title: Build the Workshop Before the Software Factory — Armin Ronacher, Earendil (AI Engineer / Code Summit 2026)
items.summary: Real session data from Earendil's own Pi coding agent: the harness hasn't changed in a year, but the models have — correction rate keeps dropping, and the 90th-percentile task now runs 14 minutes versus 2.5 minutes a year ago. Of 141 projects he's started, only 10-15 stay actively maintained. His argument: human attention, not agent capability, is now the bottleneck. Judged from the video's own transcript, read in full via YouTube's transcript panel (TubeAlfred was not available this run).
items.why: One of the most data-grounded 'what's actually changed in agentic coding' talks around right now, from someone who ships a coding agent himself.
items.action: 20 minutes — the chapters on 'knowing when to push back on the agent' (7:47) and 'executive summaries instead of reading code' (10:02) are the most immediately applicable.

items.title: How To Build Self-Improving AI Agents with Claude (Stanford's Method) — Austin Marchese
items.summary: Walks through a concrete generator/verifier/coach architecture for self-improving Claude agents, based on Stanford's course on the topic: a coach proposes one change at a time into a separate candidate file next to the live one, never rewriting what already works. Three levels: you suggest the improvement, AI suggests and you approve, or AI improves itself unsupervised. Judged from description, chapters, and comments (TubeAlfred unavailable this run, disclosed fallback). One brief affiliate mention near the top of the description; the 16-minute body isn't sponsor content.
items.why: The 'coach writes to a candidate file, never the live one' pattern is the single most copy-pasteable idea here.
items.action: 17 minutes — skip to Step 3 (6:42, 'Add the Coach') if you already have a working generator/verifier pair.

eval.reason: Concrete, genuinely new technique (3-level self-improvement framework), not a rehash.
